ruleIntents.intent: The rule statically inspects the meta viewport element's `content` attribute and checks that it does NOT lock out user zoom. It parses the content string into key/value pairs and looks only at two keys — `user-scalable` and `maximum-scale` — applying the CSS @viewport translation. Expectation 1 (user-scalable): passes if user-scalable is undefined, OR is `yes`/`device-width`/`device-height`, OR is a number whose magnitude is >= 1 (i.e. NOT strictly between -1 and 1 exclusive); fails for `no`, `0`, `0.5`, or invalid strings, since those translate to user-zoom: fixed. Expectation 2 (maximum-scale): passes if maximum-scale is undefined, OR `device-width`/`device-height`, OR negative, OR a number >= 2; fails if it caps zoom below 200% (e.g. 1.5) or is an invalid/non-numeric token (which the parser coerces to a small/zero max-zoom). A target must pass BOTH expectations to pass. In plain terms: does the viewport meta tag let a user pinch/zoom to at least 200%? It is a pure DOM-string check — no rendering, no measurement.
ruleIntents.scLimb: This is the critical nuance: despite the corpus frontmatter tagging it 1.4.10, the rule's own Accessibility Requirements Mapping makes 1.4.4 Resize text (Level AA) the PRIMARY/in-scope requirement that a failed outcome fails. 1.4.10 Reflow is listed only as a SECONDARY/related requirement that the rule "was not designed to test directly" — the rationale being that a page which cannot be zoomed to 200% often also fails to reflow, but "most failed examples [actually] satisfy" 1.4.10. So for 1.4.10 specifically, this rule exercises no real limb of the SC directly. The relevant 1.4.10 sub-clause it brushes against is the requirement that content be presented "without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions" at 320 CSS px width / 256 CSS px height (the 400% zoom / 1280px@100% equivalence). The viewport zoom-lock is a proxy: blocking pinch-zoom is the mobile mechanism by which a developer would prevent the reflowed/zoomed presentation 1.4.10 demands. But the rule never tests the 320x256 reflow condition itself.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to each `content` attribute that (a) is on a `<meta>` element whose `name` attribute equals `viewport`, AND (b) whose value contains at least one `maximum-scale` or `user-scalable` key (after parsing the content into key/value pairs). If neither key is present, the rule is inapplicable. Inapplicable cases: no viewport meta element at all; a viewport meta with no content attribute; a viewport meta whose content only sets other keys like `width=device-width`; or an empty content string.
ruleIntents.expectation: Each test target must satisfy BOTH expectations. Expectation 1 (user-scalable): user-scalable is not defined, OR equals yes/device-width/device-height, OR is a number not strictly between -1 and 1 (so |n|>=1). Expectation 2 (maximum-scale): maximum-scale is not defined, OR equals device-width/device-height, OR is negative, OR is a number >= 2. A target that violates either (e.g. user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1.5) fails. Outcome mapping for the primary SC: any failed outcome means 1.4.4 is NOT satisfied; all-passed or inapplicable means "needs further testing" (a pass is necessary but not sufficient).
scenarioTypesPresent: user-scalable allows zoom: =yes (Passed 1), =5 i.e. number magnitude>=1 (Passed 2)
maximum-scale allows zoom: =2.0 exactly at 200% threshold (Passed 3), =-1 negative (Passed 4), =device-width keyword (Passed 5)
user-scalable blocks zoom: =no (Failed 1), =0.5 fractional <1 (Failed 2), =invalid non-numeric token (Failed 3)

maximum-scale blocks zoom: =1.5 caps below 200% inside a multi-key content string with user-scalable=yes & initial-scale=0.8 (Failed 4), =yes non-numeric (Failed 5/6, duplicated), =invalid token (Failed 7)
Inapplicable: no viewport meta (Inapp 1), viewport meta with no content attr (Inapp 2), content sets only width=device-width (Inapp 3), empty content string (Inapp 4)
syntheticNarrowness: Every example is a near-identical skeleton page (title + single 'Lorem ipsum' paragraph). There is zero actual content that would need to reflow, so the cases never touch the real 1.4.10 condition (no loss at 320x256 CSS px) — they test only the viewport string, never the rendered reflow behavior the SC is about.

The rule and its tests are fundamentally about MOBILE pinch-zoom suppression, yet the rule's own Accessibility Support notes desktop and most modern mobile browsers ignore/override the viewport zoom lock — so a 'fail' here may not reflect any real user-facing 1.4.10 barrier; the tests never establish whether reflow actually breaks.

maximum-scale=1.5 is the only example of capping-below-200%; there's no coverage of borderline values like 1.99, 1.0, or maximum-scale combined with a large minimum-scale, nor of initial-scale interactions that effectively raise the floor.

Single-key minimalism: most passing/failing cases isolate one key in the content string. Only Failed 4 combines multiple keys, and there the passing user-scalable=yes does NOT rescue the failing maximum-scale=1.5 — but the tests don't probe the inverse (a permissive maximum-scale with a blocking user-scalable) or other key-ordering/precedence permutations.

No coverage of malformed/edge syntax variety: duplicate keys, whitespace/casing variants (User-Scalable vs user-scalable), missing values, semicolon vs comma separators, trailing commas, or content with quotes — all of which real-world parsers (and the non-fully-specified content parsing the rule itself flags) handle differently.

No coverage of CSS @viewport / @media equivalents, viewport set via JavaScript after load, multiple viewport meta tags, or framework-injected/CMS-injected viewport tags (e.g. theme defaults appending user-scalable=no) — the common real-world ways this defect actually appears.
Failed Examples 5 and 6 are exact duplicates (both maximum-scale=yes), inflating apparent coverage without adding a distinct scenario.

All pages are well-formed single-document HTML with the meta in <head>; no iframes, no shadow DOM, no SPA route changes, no responsive sites where reflow at 320px is actually exercised — so even as a proxy the cases never validate the link between viewport lock and a real reflow/resize failure.

scLimbsCoveredByACT: PARTIAL / INDIRECT ONLY — zoom-suppression as a proxy. The single in-scope ACT rule b4f0c3 ('Meta viewport allows for zoom') touches the SC's precondition that users must be able to enlarge content: it detects <meta name=viewport> attribute values (user-scalable, maximum-scale) that block the user agent's ability to zoom. The Understanding intent ('let users enlarge text and other related content without having to scroll in two dimensions') depends on zoom being possible at all, so a zoom-disabling viewport is a weak signal a page may also fail Reflow.

The 320 CSS-pixel-width threshold for horizontal-language content is NAMED in b4f0c3's Assumptions/Background ('The content does not need to reflow in order to fit in an area of 320 by 256 CSS pixels'), so the numeric limb is mentioned in corpus text — but it is NOT tested by any rule or example.
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: The CORE normative requirement is entirely untested: 'content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions for: Vertical scrolling content at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels; Horizontal scrolling content at a height equivalent to 256 CSS pixels.' No rule or example actually narrows a viewport to 320px / 256px and checks for two-dimensional (horizontal+vertical) scrolling. b4f0c3 only inspects the viewport meta attribute string; it never renders, reflows, or measures.

The 256 CSS-pixel HEIGHT limb for vertical/RTL-or-vertical-language content (e.g. traditional Chinese/Japanese horizontal-scrolling layouts) is completely absent — no rule, no example, no fixture exercises vertical-writing-mode reflow.

'without loss of INFORMATION' — content disappearing after reflow (the entire premise of failure technique F102: side-column link blocks vanishing, labels replaced by placeholders, images/search fields dropped with no equivalent disclosure/link). No ACT rule or example covers content-loss-on-reflow.
'without loss of FUNCTIONALITY' — interactive controls becoming unreachable/cut off after reflow (e.g. pagination 'next' button missing, search input clipped). Untested.

The EXCEPTION clause: 'Except for parts of the content which require two-dimensional layout for usage or meaning.' None of the excepted content types are represented: data tables/grids, maps, diagrams/graphics, video & fixed-dimension media, electronic program guides, presentation/slide-deck editors, code diff (two-column) views, photo editors with persistent toolbars, rich documents with side comments.

Scope-of-exception nuance: the exception applies ONLY to the two-dimensional section, NOT to surrounding non-excepted content (heading, intro paragraph, search field, pagination around a table; paragraphs after a table). The corpus has nothing exercising 'excepted section passes but adjacent non-excepted content must still reflow.'

Page-level bidirectional scrollbars that are ACCEPTABLE because they exist only to view an excepted item (e.g. a full-width video without max-width:100%, or a scroll-contained table) vs. UNACCEPTABLE page-level 2D scroll from non-excepted text. This pass/fail distinction is wholly absent.
Carousel / horizontally-scrolling section panels each fitting within 320px (techniques G225/G206) — the pass case (panel fits 320px) and fail case (panel overflows 320px) are not represented.
Meaningful text indentation / preformatted code / nested-list hierarchy that must survive reflow (technique G224, and the 'Preformatted text conveys meaning' example) — absent.
Long unbreakable URLs/strings forcing horizontal scroll (technique C33) and truncation-with-reveal alternatives (the 'Alternative presentations to truncating content' example) — absent.
Sticky/fixed-position content (ads, toolbars, sidebars) that, while reflowing, obscures content or consumes the 320px space (the Focus-Not-Obscured overlap discussion) — absent.

All SUFFICIENT techniques as positive (passing) patterns are absent: CSS Flexbox reflow (C31), media-queries + CSS grid column reflow (C32), width/max-width/flexbox for labels+inputs (C38), client-side size/position scaling with text (SCR34), and the user-selectable non-horizontal-scroll layout option (G206). No passing responsive-design fixture exists.
Viewport-vs-resolution nuance (a page judged at any device where 320/256 can be reproduced; 200% Resize-Text vs 400% Reflow relationship) — conceptual, untested.
The IT-document/PDF reflow example ('PDF offering reflow') — out of the web scope and absent.
contentDomainsPresent: The ONLY content present is b4f0c3's inline rule examples: 16 near-identical minimal HTML documents (7 Failed, 5 Passed, 4 Inapplicable), each a with a and a single <meta name='viewport' content='...'>, over a trivial <body> of one <p>Lorem ipsum</p>.

Domain = viewport-meta-attribute string parsing only (user-scalable=yes/no/0.5/5/invalid; maximum-scale=2.0/1.5/-1/device-width/yes/invalid; missing/empty content attr). No real reflow content, no responsive layout, no CSS, no images, tables, forms, carousels, or interactive widgets.
No local test-case fixtures exist (testCaseCount: 0); the corpus directory for 1.4.10 has no rendered pages — only act-rules/pages/b4f0c3.html and its extracted markdown.
varietyGaps: BIGGEST GAP — the SC's actual mechanism is never exercised: no fixture is ever rendered and narrowed to 320px width (or 256px height) to observe whether two-dimensional scrolling appears. The whole corpus tests a static attribute string, not reflow behavior. b4f0c3 is even mapped PRIMARILY to SC 1.4.4 (Resize text); for 1.4.10 it is only a 'secondary requirement' whose own Background states 'Most failed examples satisfy this success criterion [1.4.10].' So the SC has effectively zero direct coverage.

Zero passing responsive-design fixtures: no single-column stacking, no media-query/grid reflow, no flexbox reflow, no label/input wrapping (C31/C32/C38) — the corpus cannot distinguish a genuinely-reflowing page from a non-reflowing one.

Zero coverage of the exception clause and its scoping — the richest and most error-prone part of 1.4.10 (tables/grids/maps/media/EPG/slides/photo-editors/diff-views/rich-docs-with-comments, and the rule that surrounding non-excepted content must still reflow). This is where real-world Reflow judgments are hardest, and the corpus has none of it.

Zero coverage of content-loss-on-reflow (F102): blocks/labels/images/search fields disappearing at 320px with no equivalent disclosure or link — a primary, concrete failure mode with an explicit failure technique, entirely unrepresented.
Zero coverage of the 256px height / vertical-writing-mode (RTL/vertical-language, horizontally-scrolling) limb — half the SC's normative threshold has no example at all.

No content-domain variety: every example is 'Lorem ipsum' in one paragraph. Missing entirely: long unbreakable URLs/strings (C33), preformatted code & meaningful indentation/nested lists (G224), horizontally-scrolling carousel panels at 320px (G225/G206), truncation-with-reveal patterns, and sticky/fixed overlay content (Focus-Not-Obscured overlap).

No pass/fail PAIRS around the acceptable-vs-unacceptable bidirectional-scrollbar distinction (page-level 2D scroll OK only because of an excepted video/table vs. NOT OK because non-excepted text overflows) — arguably the single most nuanced judgment in the Understanding doc.

aspects.title: Non-excepted content forces a horizontal scrollbar at 320 CSS px (fixed-width container, non-wrapping layout, layout-table-as-prose)
aspects.description: The defining 1.4.10 failure: when the page is rendered at a width equivalent to 320 CSS px (the 1280px-at-400% equivalent), some section of NON-excepted content forces two-dimensional scrolling. Triggers include a fixed-width container (e.g. width:680px), a body/wrapper min-width, a flex/grid row that refuses to wrap, absolutely-positioned off-canvas content, or a layout table (a <table> used only to position prose side-by-side) that wrongly relies on the data-table exception. The viewport meta is permissive so b4f0c3 passes, yet the rendered page fails Reflow. The judgment that survives automation: a tool can see scrollWidth > clientWidth, but it CANNOT decide whether that overflow is a legitimate exception (real data table, map, video, fixed-dimension media) or a genuine failure, nor whether a wide <table> holds real tabular data versus prose that should reflow. A human must classify the overflowing element and confirm reflow is actually broken for content that should reflow.
aspects.scLimb: The core normative requirement: 'Content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions' at 320 CSS px width for horizontal-language content. The exception for sections that 'require two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality' governs which overflow is permitted.
aspects.whyUncovered: The lone ACT rule b4f0c3 is a pure DOM-string check of the viewport meta content attribute; it never renders the page, never sets a 320px viewport, and never measures overflow. Its own mapping makes 1.4.4 primary and notes 'most failed examples [actually] satisfy' 1.4.10. The synthetic corpus pages are a title plus a single short Lorem-ipsum paragraph with no content wide enough to overflow. While raw page-overflow is partly machine-detectable, the disposition (legitimate exception vs failure, data table vs layout table) is an irreducible human classification.

references.quote: This criterion requires non-excepted sections of content that are written in horizontal languages reflow when narrowed to a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels.

When lines of text extend beyond the edge of a viewport, users will be forced to scroll back-and-forth to read line by line. This can cause them to lose their place and can significantly increase both physical and cognitive effort.
The objective of this technique is to be able to present content without introducing a horizontal scroll bar at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels

aspects.constructionStrategy: Each page must declare a permissive viewport meta (width=device-width, initial-scale=1) so b4f0c3 passes, then plant exactly one overflow trigger so the human evaluator must classify it. Provide fluid surrounding prose so only the planted element overflows. Render at ~320px to verify the horizontal scrollbar appears. Include at least one PASS control (fully fluid page) and one true-exception PASS (a real data table inside an overflow:auto scroll container while prose reflows) so the aspect tests the classification judgment, not mere overflow detection.
suggestedScenarios: Article page with permissive viewport but the main article container hard-set to width:680px, so the whole page gains a horizontal scrollbar at 320px while everything else would reflow.
Fully fluid blog post EXCEPT one pull-quote <div style='width:520px'> that pushes page width past 320px.
Two-column flex layout (display:flex, no flex-wrap) of nav + content whose columns refuse to stack at 320px and overflow horizontally.
Page whose <body> has min-width:600px in CSS so it can never reflow below 600px at any zoom.
LAYOUT table (<table> used only to place two prose paragraphs side by side) overflowing at 320px while wrongly invoking the table exception.
PASS control: identical content where a genuine data table sits inside a div{overflow:auto} scroll container and all prose reflows into the 320px column (legitimate exception, must NOT be flagged).
Sidebar set position:absolute; left:340px so it sits off-canvas at 320px, generating a page-level horizontal scrollbar.

aspects.title: F102 — content/functionality present at desktop width disappears at 320px and is not reachable by any equivalent mechanism
aspects.description: The dedicated failure technique F102: a section visible at 1280px is hidden at 320px (via display:none in a max-width media query, a collapsed sidebar, a responsive nav that drops links, a search field that vanishes, labels replaced by placeholders) WITHOUT providing the same or equivalent content through a disclosure widget, hamburger menu, dialog, icon, or link to another view. The page reflows (no horizontal scroll) and the viewport meta is fine, so it looks compliant to a tool, but information or functionality has been lost. Judging it requires comparing the desktop and narrow renderings, diffing what content is reachable, and a semantic decision about whether a replacement mechanism genuinely surfaces the same information (does that hamburger button actually expose the dropped nav links, or is it dead? is placeholder text an acceptable label substitute? does the disclosure actually contain the hidden section?).
aspects.scLimb: The 'without loss of information or functionality' half of the SC at 320 CSS px width — distinct from the two-dimensional-scrolling half. Content may legitimately be repositioned or relocated, but it must remain available.
aspects.whyUncovered: F102 has no ACT rule and zero test cases; the corpus only has b4f0c3 (viewport string). Detecting it requires rendering at two widths, diffing reachable content, and a human judgment about whether a replacement mechanism (hamburger, disclosure, link) genuinely surfaces the same information. A tool cannot decide whether a hamburger icon actually leads to the dropped links or whether placeholder text is an acceptable label substitute.

references.quote: a failure that occurs when a change of the viewport width to 320px makes content disappear that was available at wider viewport widths

This content, however, should still be available after reflow to 320px viewport width, either by being repositioned in a single column view, or through some interaction offering the information in some other way, for example, in a disclosure area, a dialog, or via a link to another view.
Labels above text inputs are hidden and replaced by placeholder text after reflow, without a technique showing dedicated labels when focusing the fields.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages that DO reflow cleanly at 320px (no horizontal scroll, permissive viewport) so the only issue is lost content. Hide a meaningful section via @media (max-width:400px){...display:none}. Vary whether an equivalent exists: FAIL = no replacement at all or a dead/decorative replacement (hamburger with no wired menu); PASS = a working disclosure/menu/link that genuinely reveals the same content. Force the evaluator to actually check whether the alternative works, not just that something is hidden.
suggestedScenarios: Sidebar of 'Related articles' links hidden by @media (max-width:400px){.sidebar{display:none}} and the links appear nowhere else in the single-column view (FAIL).
Form whose labels are display:none at 320px with inputs relying on placeholder only, no <label> association, labels do not reappear on focus (FAIL).
Top nav of 6 links collapsing to a hamburger button at 320px where the button is purely decorative (no menu wired), so destinations are unreachable (FAIL).
Global search input hidden under 360px with no search icon, no menu entry, and no link to a /search page (FAIL).
PASS control: same nav collapsing to a hamburger that toggles a working <nav> disclosure containing all 6 links at 320px.
Informational chart with embedded data labels set to display:none at narrow width with no caption, longdesc, or link to a data-table alternative (FAIL).
'Download invoice' action button removed by media query at 320px while every other action remains — the function is simply gone on small viewports (FAIL).

aspects.title: Long unbroken strings (URLs, tokens, hashes, paths, emails, compound words) overflow at 320px without wrapping or a reveal alternative
aspects.description: Technique C33 addresses long sets of characters with no spaces — a displayed full URL, an API/auth key, a long hash, a deep file path, a blockchain address, a German compound word — that the browser cannot wrap (no break opportunities and no overflow-wrap:break-word / word-break applied, or white-space:nowrap forced). At 320px the one string punches out a horizontal scrollbar even though every paragraph around it reflows perfectly. The viewport meta is fine and the page is 99% fluid, so a viewport-string check sees nothing. The judgment: render at 320px to find the single overflowing element, and decide the correct disposition — whether the string may break mid-word, versus the truncate-with-reveal pattern the Understanding doc describes (truncation is only acceptable if a link or mechanism reveals the full value).
aspects.scLimb: The 'without requiring scrolling in two dimensions' requirement applied to inline text content; the related Understanding nuance that truncating content to save space is only acceptable when the full value remains available via a link or reveal mechanism.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule renders content or measures string overflow; corpus pages contain only short Lorem-ipsum with normal spaces, never a long unbreakable token. A static checker can heuristically spot a literal very-long string in markup but cannot determine whether it actually overflows at 320px (depends on font, container width, CSS) nor whether the surrounding design already wraps it nor whether a truncation has a valid reveal — this needs visual measurement plus judgment.

references.quote: Long sets of characters without a space, such as URLs shown as content, can break reflow when the page is zoomed.

The objective of this technique is to present URLs without introducing a horizontal scroll bar at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels or a vertical scroll bar at a height equivalent to 256 CSS pixels.

A web page presents long strings of text which are truncated to save space. E.g., user generated content that does not fit into the space allocated for the interface's design, or authentication keys which do not wrap

aspects.constructionStrategy: Permissive viewport, fully fluid layout, then embed exactly one long unbreakable string with break opportunities suppressed (raw string with no spaces, or white-space:nowrap, or <pre>). Render at 320px and confirm only that element overflows. Vary disposition: FAIL = string overflows with no wrap and no reveal; PASS = same string with overflow-wrap:break-word, OR truncated-with-ellipsis but accompanied by a working 'show full' link/button. Test that the evaluator distinguishes a wrapped/revealed string from a truly overflowing one.
suggestedScenarios: Support page displaying a raw 180-character tracking URL as visible link text with no overflow-wrap, overflowing the 320px viewport (FAIL).
API docs page showing a 64-character bearer token in <code style='white-space:nowrap'>, forcing horizontal scroll at 320px (FAIL).
User-profile page echoing a very long email address / handle with no break opportunities, breaking reflow (FAIL).
File manager showing a deep path /srv/.../really_long_segment_name in a <pre> that overflows 320px (FAIL).
PASS control: the same long URL with overflow-wrap:break-word so it wraps cleanly within the 320px column.
Page where a long auth key is truncated with ellipsis but a 'Reveal full key' button shows the complete value (PASS, tests the truncation-needs-alternative nuance).
Page where a long key is truncated with ellipsis and there is NO mechanism to reveal the full value (FAIL on the truncation nuance even though nothing overflows).

aspects.title: Two-dimensional-layout exception over-claimed or mis-scoped: non-excepted surroundings of a table/map/grid fail to reflow
aspects.description: 1.4.10 exempts sections that genuinely require two-dimensional layout (data tables, maps, diagrams, grids, code where indentation is meaningful, presentations). The judgment-heavy failure mode is mis-scoping: a developer lets the WHOLE page scroll in two dimensions 'because there's a table', so the heading, intro paragraph, search field, and pagination that surround the table — none of which need 2D layout — also extend off-screen and require horizontal scrolling. The Understanding doc shows exactly this pass/fail pair. Conversely, flagging content that legitimately IS a data table/map/video would be a false positive. Deciding whether a given block legitimately 'requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality', AND scoping the exception to only the excepted section, are irreducibly human contextual calls: is this <table> real tabular data or layout? is this wide block a map (exempt) or a poorly sized banner? must this heading/search/pagination reflow even though the adjacent table need not?
aspects.scLimb: The exception clause itself: 'A section of content that requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality, such as a table or map, has an exception' — plus the normative scoping that the exception 'does not automatically extend to other content that doesn't need two-dimensional scrolling'.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no rendered pages and no tables/maps/grids, so the exception is never exercised in either direction. The exception turns on the MEANING of the content and on scoping it to only the excepted section — both human judgments. Automated tools cannot distinguish a genuine data table from a layout table, nor decide that a surrounding heading/search/pagination is non-excepted and must reflow.

references.quote: A section of content that requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality, such as a table or map, has an exception to this success criterion. However, sections of content within the two-dimensional layout, such as each cell within a table, would still need to meet this success criterion.
When a section of content is excepted from Reflow, the exception does not automatically extend to other content that doesn't need two-dimensional scrolling for understanding or functionality.
Other content that is related to the table or grid, such as a preceding heading, a search field, or an accompanying pagination to load different sets of data are not excepted from meeting Reflow.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Pair a legitimately-wide excepted element (real data table, electronic program guide grid, map) with surrounding non-excepted content (heading, intro paragraph, search field, pagination). FAIL = the whole body has min-width so heading/search/pagination ALSO overflow at 320px alongside the table. PASS = the table sits in an overflow:auto scroll container while heading/search/pagination reflow into the 320px column (mirrors the Understanding reflow-table-pass-fail figure). Also include a layout-table masquerade (prose in a <table>) to test the data-vs-layout classification. The evaluator must scope the exception correctly, not just see 'a table exists, therefore exempt'.
suggestedScenarios: Data table inside a page whose <body> has min-width:900px so the H1, intro paragraph, search box, and pagination ALL overflow at 320px alongside the legitimately wide table (FAIL — non-excepted surroundings don't reflow).
PASS counterpart: same table wrapped in div{overflow:auto} while heading/search/pagination reflow into the 320px column.
Heading + search field placed on the same horizontal row as a wide grid such that the search field is pushed off-screen and cut off at 320px (FAIL, mirrors the Understanding figure).
Pagination component beside a wide table where the 'Next' button is clipped off-canvas at 320px because the pagination did not reflow (FAIL).
Electronic-program-guide grid (legitimately excepted) whose individual cell content (poster art + 'how to watch' text) itself overflows 320px within the cell (FAIL — cells must still meet Reflow).
Page-level horizontal scrollbar caused by a non-excepted decorative banner the author justified as 'image, so exempt' when it is really styled text that should wrap (FAIL — wrong exception claim).
PASS control: a wide video player without max-width:100% causes a page-level horizontal scrollbar, but ALL non-excepted prose reflows within 320px (legitimate exception, must NOT be flagged).

aspects.title: Sticky / fixed-position content (headers, footers, cookie bars, chat widgets, ads) consumes or obscures the 320x256 viewport so reflowed content cannot be read
aspects.description: Headers, footers, toolbars, cookie banners, chat widgets, and fixed ads that are reasonable at desktop become viewport-eating obstructions when zoomed to a 320px-wide / 256px-tall viewport. A sticky 130px-tall header over a 256px-tall viewport leaves almost nothing to read; a fixed-bottom cookie bar plus fixed-top nav can sandwich content into a sliver; a fixed-corner ad can cover the focused link, providing no way to dismiss it without keyboard-navigating to its close button. The Understanding doc's Focus-Not-Obscured overlap section and technique C34 both call for un-fixing these at small sizes. The page reflows horizontally (no h-scroll) and the viewport meta is permissive, so tools see nothing — but the rendered experience is broken. Judging it requires rendering at the narrow viewport (especially the 256px height) and a visual proportion assessment of how much readable space the sticky elements leave and whether they obscure content or keyboard focus.
aspects.scLimb: The 'without loss of information or functionality' requirement as it interacts with the SC's overlap with Focus Not Obscured: sticky/fixed regions that, at the reflow viewport, block so much of the screen that content cannot be read or functionality cannot be reached.
aspects.whyUncovered: Corpus pages have no sticky/fixed elements and are never rendered at 256px height. C34 is advisory with no ACT rule. The harm — a sticky element leaving too little room, or covering content/focus — is a visual proportion judgment at a specific small viewport; there is no static signal, and position:sticky/fixed are perfectly valid and ubiquitous, so their mere presence cannot be flagged. Only a human looking at the rendered narrow viewport can judge whether too little remains.

references.quote: when using mobile devices in landscape orientation or when zooming in on the desktop, sticky regions may block a big portion of the screen: the height of the sticky region may leave only a small part of the screen for the display of page content.

Such sticky or fixed content can pose significant issues for those who would benefit from Reflow, as aside from obscuring keyboard focus, such sticky or fixed content can make reading content difficult if not impossible.
It is strongly suggested that at smaller viewport sizes that such components are modified to have static positioning, or their display can be toggled by the user.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Permissive viewport, content that reflows horizontally fine. Add fixed/sticky chrome sized to eat the narrow viewport: a position:sticky header ~130px tall, a position:fixed bottom cookie bar, a fixed-corner ad/chat widget. Test BOTH the 320px width and the 256px height conditions. FAIL = the sticky chrome leaves a tiny readable sliver or covers content with no dismiss. PASS control = C34 pattern that un-fixes (position:static) the chrome via a min-height media query at the small viewport, OR a user-dismissible banner. Make the evaluator judge readable-space proportion, not the mere presence of position:sticky.

aspects.title: Horizontally-scrolling carousel where an individual panel does not fit within 320 CSS px (G225)
aspects.description: Horizontally-scrolling carousels are explicitly allowed: the strip scrolls horizontally to move between panels, but EACH individual panel must fit within 320 CSS px so the user need only scroll vertically to read one panel's content. The Understanding doc gives a pass (each home-listing panel fits 320px) and a fail (the second panel's content does not fit 320px). The failure is subtle: the carousel mechanism is fine and most panels fit, but one over-stuffed panel (longer text, an extra-wide image, a wider card) forces horizontal scrolling WITHIN that panel. Catching it requires rendering at 320px, advancing through each panel, and judging per-panel whether its content overflows — AND judging that the horizontal strip-scroll itself is the intended carousel navigation and NOT the violation. A tool cannot tell which overflow is 'the carousel working' versus 'a panel too wide'.
aspects.scLimb: The single-direction-scrolling requirement applied to carousel/panel widgets: the strip may scroll horizontally to change panels, but each panel's content must be readable with vertical-only scrolling within 320 CSS px.
aspects.whyUncovered: No carousels exist in the corpus and nothing is rendered. G225 has no ACT rule. The distinction between acceptable strip-level horizontal scrolling (navigation between panels) and unacceptable within-panel horizontal scrolling requires interpreting the widget's purpose and inspecting each panel individually at 320px — beyond static markup analysis.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build a real horizontal carousel (overflow-x:auto strip of panels). PASS = every panel sized so its content fits 320px (e.g. width in vw, or 300px cards reading top-to-bottom). FAIL = one rogue panel over-stuffed (a 420px card, a 360px embedded image, or a long unbreakable headline) so that panel forces within-panel horizontal scroll at 320px. Verify by scrolling the strip to each panel at a 320px viewport. The evaluator must NOT flag the strip-scroll itself, only the over-wide panel.

aspects.title: Preformatted text / nested-list / code indentation: distinguishing meaningful (excepted) layout from gratuitous non-wrapping that should reflow
aspects.description: Lists and code blocks often rely on indentation to convey hierarchy or meaning (nested <ul> levels, Python block structure, ascii art). Where indentation is genuinely meaningful, the section may legitimately need two-dimensional scrolling and is excepted (G224 / the Understanding 'Preformatted text conveys meaning' example). The judgment-heavy failure: a developer wraps ordinary prose in <pre> or applies white-space:nowrap to text whose layout carries NO meaning, so it refuses to wrap and overflows 320px when it should simply reflow — OR conversely, genuinely meaningful indented code that is force-flattened, losing meaning. Deciding whether the layout's meaning would be lost by wrapping (exempt) versus whether the non-wrapping is gratuitous (must reflow) is a semantic content call no tool can make. G224 also notes the conforming middle path: keep meaningful indentation but reduce it at zoomed levels and allow each nested level to be horizontally scrolled into view while its items read vertically.
aspects.scLimb: The exception for content where 'consistent orientation... is important for understandability, functionality, or both' applied to preformatted/indented text, and the corresponding requirement that text whose layout carries no meaning must reflow (wrap) at 320px.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus has only plain Lorem-ipsum prose, no <pre>, code, or nested lists, and nothing is rendered. G224 has no ACT rule. Whether indentation/non-wrapping is meaningful (exempt) or gratuitous (must wrap) depends on reading and understanding the content's semantics — a tool sees white-space:pre and cannot decide if flattening would destroy meaning.

references.quote: The presentation of text where the layout has specific meaning, such as code indentation for Python or "ascii art" as just two examples, would lose meaning if the layout were not presented correctly. This success criterion does not apply where that meaning would be lost. However, this is not the case for most other instances of text where text wrapping can be applied without loss of meaning.

There can be instances where indentation of text is considered important to the presentation and understandability of the text content. If the indentations were to be removed, then meaning or functionality could suffer.

the indentation of code blocks like these could be adjusted at different viewport sizes... each nested list can be horizontally scrolled into view. Only vertical scrolling is necessary to read the content of list items within each specific nested list level.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Pair a meaningful case (real Python or nested-list where indentation is structural) against a gratuitous case (ordinary prose in <pre> or white-space:nowrap). PASS-by-exception = genuine indented code/ascii-art that overflows but whose meaning would be lost if wrapped (legitimately excepted). PASS-by-technique = G224 pattern where meaningful indentation is reduced via media query and each nested level scrolls into view while its items read vertically. The evaluator must read the content to decide which side of the line each case falls on.

A code listing where line-wrapping is NOT essential and no wrap/mechanism is provided, overflowing 320px (FAIL — wrappable code should wrap or offer a wrap toggle).

At 320px the single word is 716px wide and forces a page-level horizontal scrollbar. Long-tail i18n case.
pages.mechanism: A real German compound word with no internal spaces has all break opportunities removed (keep-all + hyphens:none + overflow-wrap:normal), so the one word cannot reflow within 320 CSS px; probe confirmed document 755px and that neutralizing only span.defterm returns the page to exactly 320px. German morphology genuinely produces such single words, which rely on hyphenation or overflow-wrap that the author globally disabled.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: b4f0c3 passes (zoom allowed); the word is valid text so no markup linter objects. Tools do not render at 320px to measure single-token overflow and have no model of German morphology to know word-break:keep-all is fatal on a 79-letter compound while harmless on a 6-letter term elsewhere on the same page. Needs rendering plus linguistic/visual judgment.

citation.quote: By default, a long line of text will wrap to fit within the available viewport. For text written in left-to-right (LTR) and right-to-left (RTL) horizontal languages, it will wrap within the width of the viewport.

pages.scenario: CI 'Build failed' dashboard whose key/value grid, SHA (overflow-wrap:anywhere) and main job-log viewer (pre with overflow-x:auto) all reflow correctly, but a later hand-added 'Failing artifact' callout shows a ~155-char deep filesystem path in a bare <pre> with default white-space:pre and no scroll container. At 320px this one <pre> forces a page-level horizontal scrollbar. Mid case.
pages.mechanism: A <pre> inherits white-space:pre and refuses to wrap the long no-space path, and (unlike the page's other <pre>) has no overflow-x:auto scroll container, so the page itself overflows at 320 CSS px; probe confirmed document 1337px and that wrapping ONLY pre.path returns the page to exactly 320px (sole offender), while the correctly scrollable pre.log contributes nothing. Distinct mechanism: <pre> preformatting + missing scroll container.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: b4f0c3 passes; both <pre> elements are valid markup and no linter distinguishes the scrollable one from the non-scrollable one. Tools do not render at 320px to find that pre.path overflows while the visually similar pre.log is fine, and cannot judge that a slash-delimited path is non-essential preformatting that may wrap versus ASCII art / Python indentation where layout is meaningful and the Reflow exception applies.

citation.quote: The presentation of text where the layout has specific meaning, such as code indentation for Python or "ascii art" as just two examples, would lose meaning if the layout were not presented correctly. This success criterion does not apply where that meaning would be lost. However, this is not the case for most other instances of text where text wrapping can be applied without loss of meaning.

pages.scenario: PASS control: e-commerce order-tracking page shows the SAME kind of long opaque tracking URL as visible link text in the same fluid single-column layout as case-01, but the link has overflow-wrap:break-word / overflow-wrap:anywhere (the C33-prescribed CSS). At 320px the URL wraps cleanly inside the column and the page does not scroll horizontally. Head case (correctly remediated).
pages.mechanism: With overflow-wrap:break-word/anywhere applied, the long no-space token wraps within the 320 CSS px column so the user scrolls only vertically (the reading direction); probe confirmed document width equals the 320px viewport with zero overflow. Nothing is truncated and the full URL remains the link's accessible name. Exists so the evaluator must distinguish a wrapped long string (pass) from a non-wrapping one (cases 01-04).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry: a tool that cannot detect the failure in cases 01-04 (no 320px rendering/overflow measurement) equally cannot certify this pass. b4f0c3 passes here for the same trivial zoom-allowed reason it passes on the failing pages, so the ACT result is identical across pass and fail and carries no signal about actual reflow behavior. Confirming the URL wraps requires rendering at 320px.

pages.scenario: PASS (truncation nuance): cloud console API-keys page truncates the displayed key to a 10-char prefix + ellipsis so cards never overflow, BUT provides a working 'Reveal full key' disclosure (aria-expanded/aria-controls) that swaps in the full 64-char value (which wraps via overflow-wrap:anywhere) plus a Copy button. Nothing overflows at 320px and the full value is reachable. Mid case (tests the nuance against case-07).
pages.mechanism: Truncation-to-save-space would lose the value, but a real reveal mechanism makes the full content available on the page: probe confirmed no overflow at 320px, and after clicking Reveal the element shows all 71 chars, aria-expanded flips to true, a role=status line announces the change, and the page stays exactly 320px wide (the revealed key wraps, no overflow returns). Satisfies the Understanding doc condition that truncation is acceptable only when the full value remains reachable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive overflow check sees no scrollbar and passes it for the wrong reason; it cannot evaluate the truncation nuance. Judging this correctly needs (1) noticing truncation, (2) finding the reveal, (3) confirming it exposes the full value without reintroducing overflow. No axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule does steps 1-3, and none can tell this PASS apart from case-07's identical tidy layout where the reveal is absent.

citation.quote: The content is presented as truncated, but a link is provided to a web page where the content is fully visible without truncation, or a mechanism is provided on the web page to reveal the truncated content.

pages.scenario: FAIL (truncation nuance, nothing overflows): crypto-exchange withdrawal receipt shows the destination wallet address and transaction hash middle-truncated to head…tail form (0x4e9a…b71c) with NO reveal, no copy of the full value, and no link to a block explorer. The page reflows perfectly at 320px, yet the complete identifiers a user needs for an irreversible transfer are unavailable. Long-tail counterpart to case-06.
pages.mechanism: Truncation to save space is permitted only when the full content remains reachable; here the middle of the address and hash is permanently dropped with no on-page recovery path, so information available at wider widths is lost after the truncation. Probe confirmed zero horizontal overflow at 320px, so an overflow-only check passes it — but it fails the F102 'content disappears with no equivalent alternative' condition. The DOM contains only the short string (no data-full).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse blind spot: nothing overflows, so even a hypothetical overflow checker passes. Tools have no concept that a displayed string is a lossy abbreviation of a longer value, and the DOM holds only the short string with nothing to compare against to even detect truncation. Recognizing 0x4e9a…b71c as a lossy abbreviation of an identifier the user needs, with no reveal/link to restore it, is pure human semantic judgment and the precise distinction from case-06.

citation.quote: This content, however, should still be available after reflow to 320px viewport width, either by being repositioned in a single column view, or through some interaction offering the information in some other way, for example, in a disclosure area, a dialog, or via a link to another view.

Deciding the table may 2D-scroll while heading/search/pager MUST reflow is human scoping judgment.

citation.quote: Other content that is related to the table or grid, such as a preceding heading, a search field, or an accompanying pagination to load different sets of data are not excepted from meeting Reflow. For instance, while a table may require two-dimensional scrolling to maintain its understandability, a heading or paragraph that introduce the table, or a search field and pagination component that allow users to search for or navigate to different "pages" of table content are not extended this exception.

pages.scenario: Business-banking account ledger: a wide, genuine transaction table is correctly excepted AND correctly scoped inside a focusable div{overflow:auto} region, while the account header, balance-summary cards, filter form, 'Load more' button, and disclosure note all reflow into a single 320px column. No body min-width; flex-wrap on summary/filters and max-width:320px on the load-more button mean every non-excepted region renders within 302px at a 320px viewport with zero own-scroll. pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner can detect that the table container produces a horizontal scrollbar but cannot determine whether it is legitimate (an excepted table confined to its own container, everything else reflows) or a failure (non-excepted content overflowing). Tools have no notion of 'this region is excepted data, the rest must reflow', so they would either skip Reflow or false-positive on the scrollbar. Confirming the PASS requires the same human scoping judgment as confirming a failure.

citation.quote: A data table relies on two-dimensional layout for understanding, but by presenting the table in its own scrollable container it allows other content which does not meet a two-dimensional layout exception to reflow as its containing element adjusts.

pages.scenario: Streaming TV electronic program guide (EPG): the channel x time-slot grid is a legitimate 1.4.10 exception, but one 'featured premiere' cell is built with a fixed 560px internal two-column layout (poster art beside a synopsis and 'how to watch' line, both white-space:nowrap), so that single cell's own content overflows 320px. Cells within an exempt grid must still meet Reflow.
pages.mechanism: After the user scrolls the (excepted) grid to bring the featured cell into a 320px viewport, the cell's .featured-inner is fixed at width:560px and its synopsis/how-to-watch text is white-space:nowrap, so the cell extends to right=730px with a 29px own horizontal scroll. The cell's content fails Reflow even though the grid exception is valid.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner that notices the grid's horizontal scrollbar must NOT flag it (valid exception), and has no model of 'the grid may 2D-scroll, but each cell's internal content must still reflow at 320px'. Detecting that one cell's poster+synopsis layout overruns the cell requires rendering at the target viewport plus the semantic judgment that this is a non-conforming cell inside an otherwise-exempt grid. Nothing is missing in the markup (the cell has role=article and an aria-label).

citation.quote: For example, an "electronic program guide" is a type of grid used to display media programs to stream online. It might be presented alongside other content outside of its grid-based layout. The individual cells of the program guide containing information about how to watch and poster art would be expected to fit within the required width or height.

pages.scenario: Dental-practice 'About' page lays out staff bios and service descriptions in a 1240px-wide 4-column <table> and lets the page scroll horizontally, the author reasoning 'it's a table, tables are exempt'. But it is a LAYOUT table: prose in every cell, no row/column data relationship, no <th>. Prose does not require 2D layout, so the exception does not apply and the content must reflow. Tests data-vs-layout classification.
pages.mechanism: table.team is a fixed table-layout:fixed; width:1240px holding prose paragraphs with td-only cells and no th/scope/caption. At 320px it extends to right=1425px, forcing the user to scroll horizontally to read bios that would wrap perfectly into one column. There is no two-dimensional header-to-data relationship to preserve, so the table is not 'content that requires two-dimensional layout for understanding'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An automated checker either ignores Reflow or, on seeing a <table>, may assume the exception applies. The markup is well-formed with no missing attribute.
